I think it's because you need to put in some effort to appreciate music sometimes. A lot of popular music is very easy to listen to, and when you consider that a chemical reaction actually happens inside the brain when you listen to music, its easy to see why more people would opt for the music that gives them pleasure without them having to even think about it, rather than try listening to something again, or appreciate it from a different perspective.

Music appreciation takes time to learn just like playing music. Four-chord songs are easily accessible to the novice listener so they tend to be catchy and popular. Once an artist starts applying more advanced theory to their music sometimes they put it out of reach for most. There are some bands that can get some really technical stuff into their songs and remain popular (I think Radiohead has used microtones in some of their stuff!) but that takes a whole new level of skill.

I very much agree with this. Another band I think of that does this well is Rush. When you think about it, they're progressive rock which isn't very mainstream. However, they hit all the right areas of pop music too, which makes them somewhat mainstream. There most popular songs are like progressive rock pop music.

The Beatles are probably the prime example. Back when they started out, time signature changes and complex chord progressions were a relatively new invention in pop music. Art rock was an underground, counter-culture phenomenon and the Beatles managed to make the mainstream public obsessed with it.

It's the same with other things too. Great food, beer, art, etc are often acquired tastes. I think it's because great music is often subtle, complex, or delicate in ways that require some work on the part of the listener to understand what's going on. On the other hand, all that fluff takes the McDonald's approach. It applies a formula that aims to make catchy, familiar songs. The songs hit all the right buttons but do so without any substance.

Like a surprising amount of things, the experience is based on expectation. Things that are easy for your brain to predict and/or work out the pattern to, are more rewarding up-front. It get's it's little "I did it!!" feel-good chemical celebration out of the way. When the pattern get's more complex, or chords resolve in strange ways, or they just start chucking some strangeness in there, the brain can't "get it's fix." It will still recognize and predict some stuff, but lose out on some key points in the song. The more you listen to it, the better you can remember those patterns and get back to the little chemical celebrations.

This, like a lot of drugs, has diminishing returns over time. Which is why once people start getting into "good" music, they sometimes have a harder time going back to pop/fluff/filler music. It's too easy, it's all there laid out in front of you. You know the key, get a feel for the chords, and you can predict the progression after one round of them. So the celebration is lame, because the musical puzzle was lame. So the listener goes back to "more difficult" music, to get that little high.

I went to university to study music, and once you get exposed to and understand a full gambit of music theory/ear trainging classes, a lot of music becomes super boring to listen to. 20th century theory/ear training was the most difficult pair of classes I took, but they got into all the super weird, difficult to understand, and unexpected stuff you could dream up. I'm not out listening to serialist music or anything, but I like something that subverts the expectation, or throws some curve-balls. There's music that is neat to listen to as thought experiment or whatever, but not something I would keep on my playlist, like phase music (same patterns, but in this example, one hand plays faster than the other, so the way the rythyms line up will change slowly over time).
